head:
The Hybrid Way · Training

The hybrid athlete: why endurance and strength together

You are told to choose: runner or lifter, aerobic or weights. THW starts from the opposite idea, that the two complement each other. This article tests that idea against the studies, starting with the broadest (the health of whole populations), moving down to the most precise (the order of your sessions), and looking for what is demonstrated, what is exaggerated and what is not known.

The problem

In most gyms and clubs, there are two camps. Runners, cyclists and swimmers distrust weights: they believe that gaining muscle weighs them down and that strength training "breaks" endurance. Strength people distrust cardio: they believe it eats away muscle. This fear did not come out of nowhere. A famous 1980 study did show that a person who trains hard at both makes less progress in strength than one who only does strength.8 It is often cited as proof that the two are incompatible.

But epidemiology tells a different story: when hundreds of thousands of people are followed, those who do both strength training and aerobic exercise have a lower risk of death than those who do only one.

These two stories seem to contradict each other. On one side, laboratory measurements in which the two kinds of training get in each other's way. On the other, health measurements in which they add up. Yet you have to decide how to split your training hours: if you are given five per week, how many do you put on running, how many on weights, and in what order? This article starts from that decision.

The question

Is doing both endurance and strength better for you than doing only one, and is the "interference effect" between the two large enough that you have to choose?

We proceed in six steps, from the most general to the most precise: what each quality does separately, what happens when you combine them, where the idea of interference comes from, what recent analyses say, what this changes in how you organise your sessions, and finally the objections. The answer comes after that.

What is at stake

First, there is a health stake, the most solid of all. The studies you will read each link both practices to a lower risk of death, of cardiovascular disease and, for strength, of diabetes. If the two add up, ignoring one of them means giving up part of a benefit already established by the other.

Then there is time. A working adult does not have ten hours of sport a week. If the two interfere a lot, it is better to specialise; if the effect is small, it is better to balance. Getting it wrong costs years of progress or of health benefit.

There is the performance stake. So-called hybrid events, in which you run and also carry, pull and push (such as Hyrox, CrossFit, military fitness tests), demand both qualities in the same event. Someone preparing for such an event cannot afford to choose. They need to know how to put the two together.
rest:
Step 1 of 6 · Each quality, separately

Endurance and strength each protect, but not in the same way

For endurance, the evidence is the oldest and the most abundant. In the Cleveland Clinic study, which followed 122,007 patients who had been through a treadmill test, the least fit group had a risk of death 5.04 times higher than the elite group, after adjustment for age, sex, smoking and several diseases.15 In a meta-analysis of 33 studies in healthy adults, each additional MET of endurance (a MET is the unit that expresses effort as multiples of resting energy expenditure) was associated with a risk of death multiplied by 0.87, that is 13% lower.16 Endurance is therefore measured on a scale: the fittest are compared with the least fit.

For strength, what you have just read looks different: people who do strength training exercises are compared with those who do not. Three meta-analyses point the same way. The first (Momma, 2022) pools 16 cohorts; for all-cause mortality, it covers 7 of them, 263,058 participants and 42,133 deaths, and finds a risk of 0.85 times that of people who do no strength training, that is 15% lower.1,2,3 The second (Shailendra, 2022) takes in 10 studies and finds the same value of 0.85 for six of them.4 The third (Saeidifard, 2019) aggregates 11 studies and 370,256 participants, followed for 8.85 years on average, and finds 0.79.6

Three independent meta-analyses associate strength training with a lower risk of death

All-cause mortality risk ratio, strength training versus no strength training, with 95% confidence interval (Momma 0.79 to 0.93; Shailendra 0.77 to 0.93; Saeidifard 0.69 to 0.91). A value below 1 means a lower risk. Sources: Momma et al., BJSM, 2022; Shailendra et al., Am J Prev Med, 2022; Saeidifard et al., Eur J Prev Cardiol, 2019.1,4,6

What this means

Doing a little strength training goes with a risk of death roughly 15 to 21% lower than doing none, and three different teams find the same order of magnitude. Do not compare this figure with the endurance one: the 5.04 compares the bottom and the top of a fitness scale, the 0.85 compares "a little" with "nothing". The two are not measured with the same ruler, so one is not "stronger" than the other.

In the Momma meta-analysis, strength training goes with a diabetes risk of 0.83 times that of non-practitioners (0.77 to 0.89), a cardiovascular risk of 0.83 (0.73 to 0.93), a total cancer risk of 0.88 (0.80 to 0.97), but no reduction for cancers of the colon, kidney, bladder and pancreas.1 In Saeidifard, the reduction for cancer is not significant (0.81, from 0.54 to 1.20). The signal is clear for all-cause mortality and diabetes, more fragile for cancer.6

As for mechanism, VO2max sums up the work of the heart, vessels and muscles, and training increases the volume of blood ejected at each beat; without training, it falls by about 1% a year.17 For strength, the Liu study (12,591 adults) finds that strength training lowers cardiovascular risk directly and also indirectly, through a lower body mass index.7 So in part no, the two do not protect in the same way: one works through the heart and circulation, the other notably through body composition. No study read compares these mechanisms directly: this is not a complete demonstration.

If each has its share, the next question is what happens when you add them together.

Step 2 of 6 · The combination, and the dose

Both together go with a markedly lower risk than either alone

The Momma meta-analysis isolated three studies that compare people who do both strength training and aerobic exercise with people who do neither: 581,194 participants and 68,637 deaths. The all-cause mortality risk is 0.60 times that of the inactive group (interval 0.54 to 0.67), that is 40% lower. For cardiovascular deaths it is 0.54 (0.41 to 0.70), and for cancer deaths 0.72 (0.53 to 0.98).1,3 Saeidifard and colleagues find 0.60 (0.49 to 0.72) for all-cause mortality, and 0.43 (0.27 to 0.70) for cardiovascular deaths.6

A summary of the Shailendra work, published by the Cooper Institute, separates the three groups. Compared with people who do neither strength training nor moderate to vigorous activity: strength training alone goes with 18% fewer deaths, aerobic activity alone with 25% fewer, both with 40% fewer.5

Doing both goes with a lower risk of death than doing either one

Remaining all-cause mortality risk, calculated as 100 minus the published reduction (18%, 25%, 40%): derived, rounded figures. Source: Shailendra et al., Am J Prev Med, 2022, based on the Cooper Institute summary (second-hand reading). The activity measured is self-reported by questionnaire.4,5

What this means

Each practice takes its share, and the two together take a larger one. A quick calculation (derived, not a study result) gives an idea of how this accumulates: 0.82 times 0.75 gives 0.62, very close to the 0.60 observed for both. In other words, the two benefits look like effects that multiply, rather than one and the same effect counted twice. That is what you would expect if they act through partly different pathways, but it does not prove it.

A practical question follows: how much strength work is needed? You might think you have to devote hours to it. The studies show a different order of magnitude.

The lowest risk is found at around 30 to 60 minutes of strength work per week

Duration of strength training at which the risk is lowest in each dose-response analysis. The relationships are J-shaped (mortality, cardiovascular, cancer) or L-shaped (diabetes); the authors note that the effect of higher volumes is uncertain. Sources: Momma et al., BJSM, 2022; Shailendra et al., Am J Prev Med, 2022.1,3,4

What this means

Most of the advantage lies at a modest dose: the equivalent of one or two short sessions a week. In the Shailendra study, the reduction in risk of death is greatest around 60 minutes a week (a risk of 0.74 times that of non-practitioners, with an interval of 0.64 to 0.86) and diminishes beyond that.4 In the Liu study (12,591 adults), strength training of 1 to 3 sessions a week, or less than 60 minutes in total, goes with a risk of cardiovascular events 40 to 70% lower than no strength training, even after accounting for aerobic exercise, whereas 60 minutes or more show no significant further reduction.7 Momma, for his part, considers at least two days a week reasonable.2

This should be read with caution: the Liu study rests on 205 cardiovascular events and 276 deaths, with exposure reported by questionnaire, and the Momma authors consider the effect of high volumes uncertain.1,7 A small dose already brings a great deal, with no evidence that much more is needed for health.

Health therefore argues for both. That leaves the 1980 objection, which claims that the two get in each other's way.

Step 3 of 6 · Where the idea of interference comes from

In the laboratory, endurance can slow strength gains: the first study and the first synthesis

The Hickson study, published in 1980, is the starting point of the whole idea. According to Nader's re-reading in Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise, it followed three groups for 10 weeks: a strength group (30 minutes a day, 5 days a week), an endurance group (40 minutes a day, 6 days a week) and a group that did both regimens.8 The result comes in two parts. First, VO2max increased by 20 to 25% in both groups that did endurance, including the one that also did strength: adding strength did not slow endurance. Second, the strength of the combined group progressed like that of the strength group for the first six to seven weeks, then levelled off and fell in the last two.8

What this means

The 1980 message is narrower than its reputation. The interference came from endurance on strength, at a high level of strength, and not the other way round. Above all, the protocol demanded very high volumes: strength almost every day and endurance almost every day, over 10 weeks. Very few people who train for their health, or even for a hybrid event, have such a programme. Nader indicates that differences in results between studies are attributed to the choice of measures, the type of exercise, age, sex, training level and duration, and that interference is real but depends on the situation, not universal.8

To go beyond a single study, a synthesis is needed. The first dates from 2012: Wilson and colleagues pooled 21 studies and 422 effect measures. For each quality, they compared three groups: strength alone, endurance alone, combined training.9 The values are effect sizes: the higher they are, the larger the gain.

In the 2012 synthesis, adding endurance reduces gains in muscle, strength and power

Mean effect sizes by training group, 21 studies and 422 measures. Source: Wilson et al., Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research, 2012 (article record). A 2014 review cites similar but slightly different values (1.22 versus 0.8 for muscle size, 1.71 versus 1.28 for strength).9,13

What this means

For muscle size, the combined group progresses about 30% less than the strength group (0.85 versus 1.23), for strength about 18% less (1.44 versus 1.76), for power about 40% less (0.55 versus 0.91): calculations derived from the effect sizes. But endurance alone (grey bars) gives almost nothing for muscle and power: the combined group stays well above it. According to the authors, interference depends on the modality (running, not cycling, significantly reduces muscle and strength), and on the frequency and duration of the endurance sessions.9

This is where the most common version of the argument stops: "the two get in each other's way, so choose". It remains to be seen whether more recent, more numerous data confirm the size of the interference.

Step 4 of 6 · What recent analyses say

On more data, interference remains visible for power but disappears for muscle and maximal strength

In 2022, Schumann and colleagues redid the work with 43 studies and 1,090 participants (590 in combined training, 500 in strength alone). For each quality, they measured the gap between the two groups, expressed in standard deviations: zero means no difference, and a negative value means that strength alone progressed more.10,11

The gap between strength alone and combined is close to zero for muscle and strength, not for power

Standardised gap between combined training and strength alone, with 95% confidence interval (-0.20 to 0.09; -0.16 to 0.18 as reported; -0.48 to -0.08; -0.62 to -0.01). In red: the intervals that do not contain zero. The average quality of the studies is 4.3 out of 10 (PEDro scale). Source: Schumann et al., Sports Medicine, 2022.10,11

What this means

For muscle and maximal strength, the 2022 synthesis finds no difference: both intervals straddle zero, and the authors write that combined training does not appear to compromise either. For power, explosive strength (jumping, sprinting, throwing), the gap is real but modest in size: -0.28, and more marked when the two kinds of training take place in the same session (-0.31); with at least three hours between them, it is no longer significant.10 The type of endurance (cycling or running), frequency, age and training level do not significantly change the results.10

Two limitations: the quality of the studies is average, and the effect of cycling alone (-0.44) disappears when one very influential study is removed. The authors also did not analyse separately athletes who were already well trained in strength.10,14

What this means

For most people, the fear that "cardio will kill my gains" is exaggerated for muscle and maximal strength. The effect exists for power (jumping, sprinting, throwing), especially when you do the two back to back without a break. For elite athletes, these studies do not allow a conclusion: no analysis devoted to them was read.

It remains to be seen how to organise sessions so that this already modest effect is smaller still.

Step 5 of 6 · Programming and hybrid athletes

Order and spacing between sessions matter little for muscle and strength, more for power

Three levers recur in the literature: the order of exercises within the session, the gap between sessions, and the amount of endurance.

Order within the session

Eddens and colleagues (2018) pooled 10 studies of at least five weeks, about 245 participants with a mean age of 31, mostly untrained or recreationally active. Doing strength before endurance gives a 6.91% greater gain in dynamic leg strength (interval 1.96 to 11.87). No effect of order is found for muscle, static strength, VO2max and fat mass.12 For most goals, order is therefore secondary. If you do the two back to back and leg strength matters, start with the weights.

Gap between sessions

In the Schumann synthesis, interference on power is significant within the same session and is no longer significant with a gap of at least three hours.10 A 2014 biology review also recommends leaving at least three hours between the two, refuelling well between sessions and placing strength with low-intensity endurance. It is also the least solid of the set: its molecular conclusions come mostly from animal studies and acute experiments in humans, and its author declares fees from a sports drink manufacturer.13

Amount of endurance

The same review places the onset of interference above about four days of endurance a week or an intensity above about 80% of VO2max, and does not observe it in a study at three days a week at 70%.13 These are thresholds from a narrative synthesis, not meta-analysis results. The author of Stronger by Science draws from the 2022 synthesis that interference is "only a small concern, for some people, sometimes", and warns against raising endurance volume too quickly in those who are already close to their recovery limit.14

What this means

The right setting is the one that does not exceed your capacity to recover. For most people, two or three endurance sessions a week and two strength sessions, spread over different days or separated by a few hours, are enough to avoid most of the interference. This is not a prescription from a trial: it is what the data read allow, with a low to moderate level of evidence.

And hybrid athletes?

Hyrox, CrossFit and military fitness tests are designed to demand both endurance (running, rowing, cycling) and strength (carrying, pulling, pushing, lifting), often in the same event and without a break. That is what they test: not the best endurance, nor the best strength, but the transition from one to the other without collapsing. I have not found, read in full and verified, a peer-reviewed study that measures their results or what predicts them: this part therefore remains reasoning, not data. The reasoning fits in one sentence: if the event demands both, preparation that develops both is consistent with it, and the analyses of step 4 indicate that this choice costs little in maximal strength and muscle. What I cannot say is which dosage gives the best results in competition.

Step 6 of 6 · The objections

What holds up when you try to demolish the conclusion, and what remains uncertain

Objection 1: people who do both are simply healthier

This is the main one. Mortality studies are observational studies: they show that two things go together. A person who does strength training and cardio probably leads a healthier life in other respects. The Momma authors say so: exposure is reported by questionnaire, the studies are few, the results may be overestimated by publication bias, most come from the United States, and the certainty of evidence (GRADE) is very low for most outcomes and low for diabetes.1 What the studies allow us to say: both practices go with a lower risk. They do not allow us to say by how much the training itself lowers it.

Objection 2: can't strength training replace cardio?

No: Momma writes that strengthening should not replace aerobic exercise.2 In the Shailendra summary, strength training alone goes with 18% fewer deaths, aerobic alone with 25%, both with 40%.5 This is the result that most directly supports the THW line.

Objection 3: is interference really that small?

It is small for muscle and maximal strength, according to the 2022 synthesis, but not zero for power. Moreover, the 2012 synthesis found a clearer one, and the 2022 one relies on studies of average quality (4.3 out of 10).9,10 The populations studied are largely untrained or recreational people: for an elite athlete, we do not know.12 The proposed mechanism (a signalling pathway, AMPK, that would slow muscle building) is still described as hypothetical by its own authors.8,13

The answer to the problem

We posed a question: is doing both endurance and strength better for you than choosing one, and is interference large enough to force you to choose?

Are the two together better for health? Yes, and this is the best-supported point. In three independent meta-analyses, strength training alone goes with 15 to 21% lower risk of death, and the combination with aerobic exercise with about 40% lower. This comes from observational studies (low to very low GRADE certainty for strength training): it is a link that is solid in direction and in order of magnitude, and not proof that training causes all of the reduction.

Does interference force you to choose? No, for most people. It exists: it was observed as early as 1980, and the 2022 synthesis finds it again for power, especially when the two kinds of training follow each other without a break. It is not found for muscle and maximal strength. It is reduced by simple means: separating the sessions, not raising endurance volume too fast, doing strength before endurance if the two are in the same session and leg strength matters. What is not demonstrated: the same conclusion in elite athletes, and the optimal dose for specific hybrid events.

What is exaggerated. Saying that cardio "kills gains" (no, for muscle and maximal strength), or that the two "get in each other's way so choose" (this ignores the health benefit of the combination).

What to put in place

The following actions are ordered. The doses of strength and endurance are taken from the studies read; the testing frequencies are an editorial choice based on the length of the training protocols and on test noise, not on a study.

  1. Measure both qualities with the tests on the page.The endurance test and the strength test each give a reference point, and together they show whether your profile leans to one side. A field test estimates, it does not diagnose.19 The norm table and protocol of the THW tests were not provided for this version: the article promises no result.
  2. Aim for at least two short strength sessions a week.The analyses place most of the benefit at around 30 to 60 minutes a week, and Momma considers at least two days reasonable.1,2,4 No need for ten hours in the gym.
  3. Keep a regular endurance base.The activity recommendations cited by a cardiologist in the specialist press are 150 minutes a week of moderate intensity, or 75 minutes of vigorous intensity.18 Do not replace one with the other: the data show a benefit in having both.2,5
  4. Organise sessions to limit interference.If possible, separate them by at least three hours or put them on different days, especially if your priority is power. If you do the two back to back and leg strength matters, start with the weights.10,12 Raise endurance volume gradually.14
  5. Retest every 8 to 12 weeks, under the same conditions.Same surface, same time of day, same warm-up. For the Cooper test, the variation from one attempt to the next is about 52 metres in runners: below that, a difference proves nothing.19 If one of the two scores goes up while the other drops markedly, that is the signal to look at first: the volume on one side may have taken over.

A very low score, chest pain or abnormal breathlessness justify medical advice before you train harder.

What these figures do not say
  • The links with mortality come from observational studies, with activity reported by questionnaire and a low or very low certainty of evidence.1,5
  • I have not read a source on the effect of strength training on bones or on physical function over the course of ageing: the article does not claim them.
  • No study read concerns elite athletes or the hybrid events themselves.

Frequently asked questions

Does cardio make you lose muscle?

In the 2022 synthesis, adding endurance does not change muscle size compared with strength alone. It may slow power, especially in the same session.10

Is it better to do strength before or after cardio?

For most measures, order makes no difference. For dynamic leg strength, strength first gives a better gain in the data read.12
